title: What makes a strategy rules-based

inOneLine.simple: A rules-based strategy writes down exactly when to enter, when to exit and how much to risk, so two people applying it to the same chart make the same trades.
inOneLine.balanced: Exact rules can be tested on past and simulated charts, and the results can be compared fairly. Vague rules cannot: the result depends on who applies them and in what mood.

explain.simple: "Buy when the trend looks strong" is an opinion. "Buy on a close above the highest high of the previous 20 candles" is a rule: anyone can check whether it happened. A full rule set covers the entry, the exit, the [[stop-loss]], the position size and which markets and [[timeframe|timeframes]] it applies to. This module teaches two well-known families, moving-average trend following and channel breakouts, as simplified educational versions. Named historical versions of these systems are added to TradeLab only after a person has checked them against reliable sources.
explain.balanced: Rules make testing possible, but they do not make a strategy good. A rule set needs enough trades to judge ([[sample-size]]), results measured in R so different trades compare fairly ([[r-multiple]]), and costs included. Trend and breakout rules usually lose more often than they win and rely on a few large winners, so a long [[losing-streak]] is part of their normal behaviour. Named historical versions of these systems are added to TradeLab only after a person has checked them against reliable sources.

assumptions: Rule: enter long on a close above the highest high of the previous 20 candles
Before day 1, the highest high of the previous 20 candles is 1.1180
steps: Day 1 closes at 1.1175. That is below 1.1180, so there is no entry, even though the day's high reached 1.1190.
Day 2: the previous 20 candles now include day 1, so the level rises to 1.1190. Day 2 closes at 1.1195, above 1.1190: the rule triggers.
The order fills at day 3's open, because the signal is only known once day 2 has closed.
Anyone applying the rule to these candles reaches the same answer: that is what makes it testable.

assumptions: 30 replay trades following one rule set (illustrative practice results, not real performance)
steps: Win rate = 11 ÷ 30 ≈ 37%: most trades lost, yet the total is positive in this sample.
30 trades is a small sample. A few different results would change the conclusion, so this says little about the future.

explainSimpler: A recipe instead of a feeling: if the rule is written exactly, anyone can follow it and check it.
commonMistake: Changing the rules after every loss. Each change creates a new strategy with no test behind it, and the losing streaks that trend and breakout rules normally have are never sat through long enough to judge them.

quickCheck.prompt: Which rule is specific enough to test?

options.text: Buy on a close above the highest high of the last 20 candles
options.explanation: Right: anyone can check whether it happened, so the result does not depend on who applies it.

options.text: Buy when the trend feels strong and the news is good
options.explanation: No: "feels strong" and "good news" mean different things to different people.
No: "building" is not defined, so two people would trade it differently.

quickCheck.prompt: 30 trades: 11 winners averaging +2.1R and 19 losers of −1R. What is the expectancy per trade?

options.explanation: No: that is the average win minus the average loss (2.1 − 1), which ignores how often each happens.
No: a low win rate can still give a positive total when winners are larger than losers.

doItNow.instructions: Open Replay with the Breakout scenario. Before you start, write your entry, exit, stop and size rules in one sentence each. Take 5 trades using only those rules, and note any moment you wanted to break them.

homework: Rewrite one vague trading idea of your own as exact rules for entry, exit, stop and size.
